title: Check Your Pantry: Great Value Fruit Cocktail Recalled Over Possible Lead Contamination
excerpt: Pacific Coast Producers recalled about 1,800 cases of Great Value fruit cocktail — more than 40,000 cans — after an FDA enforcement report flagged possible lead contamination.
content:
More than 40,000 cans of Great Value fruit cocktail sold at Walmart have been recalled because they may be contaminated with lead, according to a U.S. Food and Drug Administration enforcement report published this week.

Pacific Coast Producers recalled about 1,800 cases of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate. The recalled product came in 15-ounce cans with a best-by date of September 1, 2027, and the lot code 6FCB 04 C2263. The recall is listed as a Class II event, meaning eating the product may cause temporary or medically reversible health consequences, or that the probability of serious harm is remote.

That classification should not be read as reassurance where lead is concerned. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states there is no safe level of lead exposure. Children face the most risk from lead exposure, but ingesting lead can still harm adults. Lead is a particular concern precisely because it is invisible — a contaminated can looks, smells and tastes like any other.

What to check

The check is specific: Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate, 15-ounce cans, best-by September 1, 2027, lot code 6FCB 04 C2263. Cans that do not match that lot code are not part of this recall. Shoppers who find a matching can should not eat it; the standard course for a recalled food product is to return it to the store where it was purchased.

Great Value is Walmart's store brand, sold at Walmart stores across Texas and the country, which is why a recall of 1,800 cases reaches far beyond any single store. Webb County shoppers who stock canned fruit for school lunches, food pantries or hurricane-season supplies are among those who should check.

Questions worth asking

How did lead reach a canned fruit product, and how many cans were sold before the recall? The enforcement report identifies the product and the lot; it does not yet answer how the contamination occurred or whether any illnesses have been linked to it. Those answers matter because lead exposure in children can have lasting effects, and because a Class II label can make a recall sound routine when the contaminant is anything but.
